claim: The C. elegans nervous system is composed of 302 neurons.
source: Its nervous system is composed of only 302 neurons, which fall into a wide range of 118 anatomically defined and molecularly distinct neuron classes (Hobert et al., 2016; White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about C. elegans cited from published literature.

claim: The C. elegans nervous system contains 118 anatomically defined and molecularly distinct neuron classes.
source: Its nervous system is composed of only 302 neurons, which fall into a wide range of 118 anatomically defined and molecularly distinct neuron classes (Hobert et al., 2016; White et al., 1986).
evidence: This classification is cited from published literature and used throughout the manuscript.

claim: UNC-86 and MEC-3 homeodomain proteins heterodimerize to directly control the expression of scores of reporter genes that define the phenotype of differentiated touch sensory neurons.
source: Both TFs were found to heterodimerize to directly control the expression of scores of reporter genes that define the phenotype of differentiated touch sensory neurons (Duggan et al., 1998; Xue et al., 1993; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies demonstrating the heterodimerization and regulatory function.

claim: Terminal selectors are continuously expressed throughout the life of the respective neuron types.
source: The continuous expression of these factors throughout the life of the respective neuron types combined with conditional gene removal has further illustrated that these factors are not only required for initiation of the respective neuron type-specific gene batteries but also continuously required to maintain their expression.
evidence: This is stated as a general property of terminal selectors based on experimental evidence.

claim: Terminal selectors are required for both initiation and maintenance of neuron type-specific gene batteries.
source: The continuous expression of these factors throughout the life of the respective neuron types combined with conditional gene removal has further illustrated that these factors are not only required for initiation of the respective neuron type-specific gene batteries but also continuously required to maintain their expression.
evidence: This is supported by conditional gene removal experiments cited in the text.

claim: TargetOrtho2 scans eight nematode genomes including Caenorhabditis elegans, Caenorhabditis briggsae, Caenorhabditis remanei, Caenorhabditis japonica, Pristionchus pacificus, Pristionchus exspectatus, and Ascaris lumbricoides.
source: TargetOrtho2 scans eight nematode genomes including members of diverse clades separated by 500 million years of evolution (Caenorhabditis elegans, Caenorhabditis briggsae, Caenorhabditis remanei, Caenorhabditis japonica, Pristionchus pacificus, Pristionchus exspectatus, Ascaris lumbricoides) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The nematode genomes scanned by TargetOrtho2 are separated by 500 million years of evolution.
source: TargetOrtho2 scans eight nematode genomes including members of diverse clades separated by 500 million years of evolution (Caenorhabditis elegans, Caenorhabditis briggsae, Caenorhabditis remanei, Caenorhabditis japonica, Pristionchus pacificus, Pristionchus exspectatus, Ascaris lumbricoides) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This evolutionary distance is stated as context for the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: A Gaussian process classifier (GPC) trained on motif features from UNC-3, CHE-1, and TTX-3::CEH-10 validated target gene motif feature data best distinguished true TF target genes from random genes.
source: We found that a Gaussian process classifier (GPC) trained on motif features from UNC-3, CHE-1, and TTX-3::CEH-10 validated target gene motif feature data best distinguished true TF target genes from random genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the cross-validation analysis shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: 90% of differentially expressed BDU genes have UNC-86 motif matches showing significant enrichment compared to genome-wide motif occurrences per gene.
source: We find 90% of differentially expressed BDU genes have UNC-86 motif matches (motif M03312_2.00) showing significant enrichment compared to genome-wide motif occurrences per gene (hypergeometric test p=1.54e-12).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from the motif enrichment analysis with statistical test.

claim: UNC-86 is required for the expression of 12 markers in the BDU neuron class.
source: For example, the TF UNC-86 is required for the expression of 12 markers in the BDU neuron class (Gordon and Hobert, 2015).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: ODR-7 is required for expression of ins-1 and pgp-2 reporters in AWA neurons.
source: We generated reporters for two predicted ODR-7 target genes, ins-1 and pgp-2, and found that both express in AWA, and that their expression is abrogated in odr-7 mutant animals (Figure 5, Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental result from reporter gene analysis in mutant backgrounds.

claim: CFI-1 is required for expression of unc-17 and cho-1 in PVC neurons.
source: We asked whether the three genes that define the cholinergic phenotype of PVC require cfi-1 for expression in PVC. These include the transporter and enzyme unc-17/VAChT and cha-1/ChaT (which are organized into an operon-like structure) and the choline transporter cho-1. Each of these loci contains phylogenetically conserved, TargetOrtho2-predicted bindings sites for CFI-1 and we observe loss of expression of reporters for these genes in the PVC neurons of cfi-1 mutants (Figure 5, Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental result from reporter gene analysis in cfi-1 mutant backgrounds.

claim: UNC-86 is required for expression of flp-19 and gcy-33 in URX neurons.
source: Apart from the above-mentioned genes, we examined whether the expression of two additional predicted UNC-86 target genes identified by TargetOrtho2, flp-19 and gcy-33, also require UNC-86 for expression in URX. By crossing the corresponding reporter transgenes into an unc-86 mutant background, we indeed found this to be the case (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an experimental result from reporter gene analysis in unc-86 mutant backgrounds.

claim: Mutation of the UNC-86 binding site in the cho-1 reporter results in complete loss of expression in URX.
source: Specifically, we mutated the predicted UNC-86 binding site (motif M03312_2.00) in a transgenic reporter of the choline transporter gene cho-1 and found complete loss of expression in URX (Figure 5B–D) suggesting this binding site is functional in URX.
evidence: This is an experimental result from binding site mutation analysis.

claim: Deletion of the LIM-4 binding site in the cho-1 reporter causes loss of expression in SMB neurons.
source: To assess the functional relevance of these predictions, we introduced a deletion of the LIM-4 binding site in the cho-1 reporter construct and found this mutation caused loss of expression in SMB neurons, as predicted by genetic loss-of-function analysis (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an experimental result from binding site deletion analysis.

claim: Deletion of a second higher scoring UNC-42 binding site in the cho-1 promoter results in loss of expression only in SMD neurons.
source: Deletion of a second higher scoring UNC-42 binding site in the cho-1 promoter results in loss of expression only in SMD neurons (SMB is not affected) (Figure 5B–D), as predicted by genetic loss-of-function analysis (Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an experimental result from binding site deletion analysis.

claim: The differentially expressed gene batteries of 117 of 118 neuron classes have putative terminal selector TFs based on coordinated regulatory motif signatures.
source: We find that the differentially expressed gene batteries of 117 of 118 neuron classes have putative terminal selector TFs, based on each displaying one or more 'coordinated regulatory' motif signatures (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: This is a major finding from the genome-wide motif enrichment analysis.

claim: Each neuron class-specific gene battery shows enrichment for multiple distinct DNA binding motifs (up to around 28).
source: Each neuron class-specific gene battery shows enrichment for multiple distinct DNA binding motifs (up to around 28; Figure 6A) with a total of 124 TFs contributing to these type 'coordinated regulatory' motif signatures (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 2E,F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: 124 TFs contribute to coordinated regulatory motif signatures across neuron classes.
source: Each neuron class-specific gene battery shows enrichment for multiple distinct DNA binding motifs (up to around 28; Figure 6A) with a total of 124 TFs contributing to these type 'coordinated regulatory' motif signatures (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 2E,F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: Between 8% and 36% of reporter genes whose expression is terminal selector-dependent based on mutant analysis have either no predicted binding site or a poorly ranked binding site.
source: between 8% and 36% of reporter genes whose expression is terminal selector-dependent based on mutant analysis have either no predicted binding site or a poorly ranked binding site (bottom 50% percentile of genome-wide candidate TF target genes) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the limitations of the binding site prediction approach.

claim: Of 23 ASE-expressed reporter genes that lose expression in che-1 mutant animals, four have no predicted CHE-1 binding site and four others are poorly ranked CHE-1 target genes by TargetOrtho2.
source: For example, of 23 ASE-expressed reporter genes that lose expression in che-1 mutant animals (Etchberger et al., 2007), four have no predicted CHE-1 binding site and four others are poorly ranked CHE-1 target genes by TargetOrtho2.
evidence: This is a specific example quantifying the limitations of binding site prediction.

claim: 98% of candidate terminal selector pairs show common target genes.
source: Of these candidate terminal selector pairs (where motif 1 and motif 2 have a coordinated regulatory motif signature), we find that 98% show common target genes suggesting that a combinatorial activity of TFs is the predominant mode of effector gene regulation (Figure 7C, D, E, Figure 7—source data 1, Supplementary file 2G).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cofactor analysis.

claim: UNC-3 and UNC-42 both target common effector genes in command interneurons.
source: For example, our analysis predicts that UNC-3 and UNC-42, rather than acting in parallel pathways, both target common effector genes in the command interneurons, a group of interconnected neurons controlling locomotion (Figure 7C, Supplementary File S2G).
evidence: This is a prediction from the cofactor analysis.

claim: The UNC-3::UNC-42 pair uniquely shows co-motif enrichment in all command interneuron gene batteries.
source: While many cofactor pairs are predicted to target common effector genes in one or several command interneurons, the UNC-3::UNC-42 pair uniquely shows co-motif enrichment in all command interneuron gene batteries.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the cofactor analysis.

claim: CEH-8 and CEH-32 homeodomain TFs are required to specify the RIA interneurons.
source: Another example is the predicted combinatorial activity of the CEH-8 and CEH-32 homeodomain TFs (Figure 7D, Figure 7—source data 1, Supplementary file 2D,G). Recent loss-of-function studies show that these two homeodomain TFs are required to specify the RIA interneurons (Reilly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from a recent published study.

claim: 113 of 118 neuron classes have predicted terminal selector co-regulators in which each individual TF is a predicted terminal selector with common targets.
source: Broken down by neuron class, we observe predicted terminal selector co-regulators in which each individual TF is a predicted terminal selector with common targets in 113 of 118 neuron classes (Figure 7D, E, Figure 7—source data 1, Supplementary file 2D,G).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the cofactor analysis across all neuron classes.

claim: The Brain Atlas dataset contains data for all 118 neuron classes, with each neuron class expressing on average 50 reporter genes (range 14 to 233).
source: Our latest version contains data for all 118 neuron classes, with each neuron class expressing on average 50 reporter genes (range 14 to 233).
evidence: This describes the content of the Brain Atlas dataset.

claim: Terminal selectors for all 118 neuron classes are predicted from the Brain Atlas dataset.
source: Examining all 118 neuron classes, we identified motif signatures for 136 neuronal TFs and predict terminal selectors (coordinated regulatory motif signatures) for all 118 neuron classes (Supplementary file 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the motif analysis of the Brain Atlas dataset.

claim: The proportion of genes with motifs per neuron class is highly correlated between single cell and Brain Atlas datasets (Spearman correlation = 0.80, p=0).
source: A comparison between single cell and Brain Atlas datasets shows that the proportion of genes with motifs per neuron class is highly correlated (Spearman correlation = 0.80, p=0) (Figure 8A) despite the independent nature of each dataset (marker population overlap per neuron class varies from 0% to 11%, average 4.5%).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between the two datasets.

claim: The identified motif signature model per TF per neuron class is significantly correlated between single cell and Brain Atlas datasets (Spearman correlation = 0.30, p=2.66e−38).
source: Furthermore, the identified motif signature model per TF per neuron class is significantly correlated (Spearman correlation = 0.30, p=2.66e−38) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison between the two datasets.

claim: 83% agreement of specific terminal selectors between single cell and Brain Atlas datasets is found when examining the top two predicted terminal selectors per neuron class (excluding panneuronally expressed regulators).
source: Examining the top two predicted terminal selectors per neuron class (sorted by rank sums test p-value), we find 83% agreement of specific terminal selectors between the datasets (excluding panneuronally expressed regulators) (Figure 8C, Supplementary file 3B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of terminal selector predictions between datasets.

claim: 92% agreement of terminal selectors between datasets is found when panneuronally expressed regulators are included.
source: When panneuronally expressed regulators are included in this comparison, we find 92% agreement; this increase appears to be driven by ztf-11, a TF implicated neuronal transdifferentiation (Lee et al., 2019), predicted to have a coordinated regulatory role in 73 neuron classes.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with explanation of the increase.

claim: TargetOrtho2 is approximately 50 times faster than the previous version with run times averaging 20 min per job.
source: TargetOrtho2 is approximately 50 times faster than the previous version (Glenwinkel et al., 2014) with run times averaging 20 min per job (median 17.8 min, range 8 to 80 min, FIMO p-value threshold = 1e-4).
evidence: This is a performance metric for the software tool.

claim: The coordinated regulatory principle appears to operate throughout the nervous system of C. elegans.
source: The breadth by which the coordinated regulatory principle appears to operate throughout the nervous system of C. elegans suggests that this principle may be used broadly in other organisms as well.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive analysis across all neuron classes.

claim: The coordinated regulatory principle may be used broadly in other organisms.
source: The breadth by which the coordinated regulatory principle appears to operate throughout the nervous system of C. elegans suggests that this principle may be used broadly in other organisms as well.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from C. elegans findings to other organisms.

claim: The Ets domain TF Pet1 in combination with other factors broadly coordinates expression of terminal identity markers of serotonergic neurons in the hindbrain.
source: In spite of these often encountered challenges, a few notable examples of putative vertebrate terminal selectors include the Ets domain TF Pet1, which in combination with other factors broadly coordinates expression of terminal identity markers of serotonergic neurons in the hindbrain (Spencer and Deneris, 2017)
evidence: This is cited as an example of terminal selector function in vertebrates.

claim: Several Dlx homeodomain factors directly control and maintain terminal identity features in forebrain GABAergic interneurons.
source: several Dlx homeodomain factors which directly control and maintain terminal identity features in forebrain GABAergic interneurons (Lindtner et al., 2019; Pla et al., 2018)
evidence: This is cited as an example of terminal selector function in vertebrates.

claim: Lhx2 protein functions as a terminal selector in olfactory neurons.
source: the Lhx2 protein in olfactory neurons (Monahan et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2016)
evidence: This is cited as an example of terminal selector function in vertebrates.

claim: Brn3a functions as a terminal selector in the habenula.
source: Brn3a in the habenula (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2018)
evidence: This is cited as an example of terminal selector function in vertebrates.

claim: Pitx3 homeodomain protein functions as a terminal selector in dopaminergic neurons.
source: the Pitx3 homeodomain protein in dopaminergic neurons (Smidt and Burbach, 2009)
evidence: This is cited as an example of terminal selector function in vertebrates.

claim: The homeodomain protein Crx functions as a terminal selector in photoreceptors.
source: or the homeodomain protein Crx in in photoreceptors (Corbo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited as an example of terminal selector function in vertebrates.

claim: Neuron type-specific gene batteries are defined by unique combinations of not uniquely expressed genes.
source: While each neuron type expresses a unique gene battery, each individual genetic component of a gene battery is usually expressed in more than one neuron type. For example, the biosynthetic enzymes and transporters that define a specific neurotransmitter phenotype are expressed by multiple distinct cell types (e.g. acetylcholine is used as a neurotransmitter by spinal cord motor neurons, as well as projection neurons in the basal forebrain). Hence, neuron-specific gene batteries are defined by unique combinations of not uniquely expressed genes.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about how neuron identity is defined, supported by examples.

claim: Acetylcholine is used as a neurotransmitter by spinal cord motor neurons and projection neurons in the basal forebrain.
source: For example, the biosynthetic enzymes and transporters that define a specific neurotransmitter phenotype are expressed by multiple distinct cell types (e.g. acetylcholine is used as a neurotransmitter by spinal cord motor neurons, as well as projection neurons in the basal forebrain).
evidence: This is an example of shared neurotransmitter usage across different neuron types.

claim: Terminal selectors are continuously required to maintain expression of neuron type-specific gene batteries.
source: The continuous expression of these factors throughout the life of the respective neuron types combined with conditional gene removal has further illustrated that these factors are not only required for initiation of the respective neuron type-specific gene batteries but also continuously required to maintain their expression.
evidence: This is based on conditional gene removal experiments.

claim: For 16 out of 17 cases where genetic loss-of-function analysis indicated multiple TFs control common target genes, significant co-enrichment and ranking of TargetOrtho2-predicted target genes was observed.
source: To address these possibilities, we first focused on 17 cases where genetic loss-of-function analysis has already indicated the existence of multiple TFs that are each required to control the expression of common target genes in a specific neuron type (see Hobert, 2016a for references). This included, for example, the case of the heteromerically acting TTX-3 and CEH-10 homeodomain proteins (Wenick and Hobert, 2004). For 16 out of these 17 cases, we observed significant co-enrichment and ranking of TargetOrtho2-predicted target genes, suggesting that co-expressed terminal selectors with coordinated regulatory motif signatures mainly target common effector genes (Figure 7B Supplementary file 2D).
evidence: This validates the computational predictions against known genetic data.

claim: CEH-14 and UNC-86 are predicted to co-regulate the gene battery of PHC neurons based on co-enriched binding sites.
source: For example, the CEH-14 LIM homeobox gene and the UNC-86 POU homeobox genes are predicted to co-regulate the gene battery of the PHC neurons based on the presence of co-enriched binding sites in the PHC gene battery and this prediction is validated by genetic analysis that showed loss of a number of PHC markers in unc-86 and ceh-14 mutants (Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013).
evidence: This prediction is validated by cited genetic analysis.

claim: CEH-14 and CFI-1 binding sites are co-enriched in the effector gene battery of cholinergic PVC neurons.
source: Similarly, CEH-14 and CFI-1 binding sites are co-enriched in the same set of genes that constitute the effector gene battery of the cholinergic PVC neurons (see Supplementary file 2D for co-enrichment statistics) and genetic mutant analysis has previously confirmed loss of PVC marker gene expression in ceh-14 mutants (Pereira et al., 2015), and, as we have shown above, cfi-1 affects PVC marker genes (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by both computational analysis and genetic validation.

claim: ODR-7 regulates expression of the odr-10 gene in AWA neurons.
source: The odr-7 orphan nuclear hormone receptor was previously shown to regulate expression of the odr-10 gene in the AWA neurons (Sengupta et al., 1996; Sengupta et al., 1994) and to autoregulate as well (Colosimo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: ODR-7 autoregulates its own expression.
source: The odr-7 orphan nuclear hormone receptor was previously shown to regulate expression of the odr-10 gene in the AWA neurons (Sengupta et al., 1996; Sengupta et al., 1994) and to autoregulate as well (Colosimo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: TargetOrtho2 identifies phylogenetically conserved ODR-7 binding sites in both odr-10 and odr-7 itself.
source: TargetOrtho2 identifies phylogenetically conserved ODR-7 binding sites in both odr-10 and odr-7 itself and predicts significant enrichment (hypergeometric p=1.04e-7) and ranking (Wilcoxon p=2.04e-8) of gene loci among the other 353 AWA differentially expressed genes (as determined by scRNA sequencing; Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a result from the TargetOrtho2 analysis.

claim: ODR-7 is among the top two terminal selector candidates for AWA identity.
source: ODR-7 is among the top two terminal selector candidates for AWA identity (Supplementary file 2A, Supplementary file 2F).
evidence: This is a result from the ranking analysis.

claim: CFI-1 regulates the expression of nmr-1 and glr-1 ionotropic glutamate receptors in PVC interneurons.
source: Similarly, the ARID-type TF cfi-1 was previously found to regulate the expression of two ionotropic glutamate receptors in the PVC interneurons, nmr-1 and glr-1 (Shaham and Bargmann, 2002).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: UNC-86 controls cholinergic identity features of URX neurons.
source: As a third example, we considered unc-86 POU homeobox gene function in the URX neuron class. Previous work had shown that unc-86 controls cholinergic identity features of URX (Pereira et al., 2015), as well as the expression of a soluble oxygen sensor, gcy-32 (Qin and Powell-Coffman, 2004), and the neuropeptide flp-8 (Kim and Li, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from published studies.

claim: UNC-86 controls expression of the soluble oxygen sensor gcy-32 in URX neurons.
source: Previous work had shown that unc-86 controls cholinergic identity features of URX (Pereira et al., 2015), as well as the expression of a soluble oxygen sensor, gcy-32 (Qin and Powell-Coffman, 2004), and the neuropeptide flp-8 (Kim and Li, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: UNC-86 controls expression of the neuropeptide flp-8 in URX neurons.
source: Previous work had shown that unc-86 controls cholinergic identity features of URX (Pereira et al., 2015), as well as the expression of a soluble oxygen sensor, gcy-32 (Qin and Powell-Coffman, 2004), and the neuropeptide flp-8 (Kim and Li, 2004).
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: The POU4F1 derived binding motif appears in over 80% of URX genes.
source: We find that the POU4F1 derived binding motif (M03312_2.00) appears in over 80% of URX genes while the alternative C. elegans derived motif (M02244_2.00) appears in 44% of URX genes.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from motif analysis.

claim: The C. elegans derived UNC-86 motif appears in 44% of URX genes.
source: We find that the POU4F1 derived binding motif (M03312_2.00) appears in over 80% of URX genes while the alternative C. elegans derived motif (M02244_2.00) appears in 44% of URX genes.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from motif analysis.

claim: Phylogenetically conserved copies of both UNC-86 motifs are enriched in the scRNA-determined URX-specific gene battery.
source: Using TargetOrtho2 we find that phylogenetically conserved copies of both motifs are enriched in the scRNA-determined URX-specific gene battery (Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the TargetOrtho2 analysis.

claim: LIM-4 is a putative terminal selector in SMB neurons based on genetic loss-of-function data.
source: We observed that cho-1 is also a predicted target gene of LIM-4 and UNC-42, putative terminal selectors based on genetic loss-of-function data for the SMB (LIM-4: Kim et al., 2015) and SMD (UNC-42: Berghoff et al., 2021) neuron classes.
evidence: This is based on cited genetic loss-of-function data.

claim: UNC-42 is a putative terminal selector in SMD neurons based on genetic loss-of-function data.
source: We observed that cho-1 is also a predicted target gene of LIM-4 and UNC-42, putative terminal selectors based on genetic loss-of-function data for the SMB (LIM-4: Kim et al., 2015) and SMD (UNC-42: Berghoff et al., 2021) neuron classes.
evidence: This is based on cited genetic loss-of-function data.

claim: UNC-42 controls the identity of many neurons in which it is expressed.
source: Additional functional validation of our terminal selector prediction is provided in Berghoff et al., 2021, where we show that the UNC-42 homeodomain TF indeed controls the identity of the many neurons in which it is expressed, with the gene batteries of most of these neurons showing a significant DNA binding motif enrichment and TargetOrtho2 rank order of UNC-42 binding sites (Berghoff et al., 2021 accompanying manuscript).
evidence: This is cited from an accompanying manuscript.

claim: The gene batteries of most neurons expressing UNC-42 show significant DNA binding motif enrichment and TargetOrtho2 rank order of UNC-42 binding sites.
source: Additional functional validation of our terminal selector prediction is provided in Berghoff et al., 2021, where we show that the UNC-42 homeodomain TF indeed controls the identity of the many neurons in which it is expressed, with the gene batteries of most of these neurons showing a significant DNA binding motif enrichment and TargetOrtho2 rank order of UNC-42 binding sites (Berghoff et al., 2021 accompanying manuscript).
evidence: This is cited from an accompanying manuscript.

claim: Homeodomain-type TFs are prominent regulators of neuronal identity throughout the entire nervous system.
source: Many of these TFs are homeodomain-type TFs which corroborate the recently proposed hypothesis that they are prominent regulators of neuronal identity throughout the entire nervous system (Reilly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the current analysis and cited from a recent publication.

claim: Each individual neuron class in C. elegans expresses a unique combination of homeodomain TFs.
source: Many of these predicted cofactor combinations are homeodomain proteins, which is consistent with our recent finding that each individual neuron class in C. elegans expresses a unique combination of homeodomain TFs (Reilly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from a recent publication.

claim: Homeodomain codes leave phylogenetically conserved, cis-regulatory footprints in neuron type-specific gene batteries.
source: Our binding site analysis demonstrates that those 'homedomain codes' leave phylogenetically conserved, cis-regulatory footprints in neuron type-specific gene batteries and corroborate their critical role in neuronal identity specification.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the binding site analysis.

claim: Not all C. elegans TFs currently have well-defined binding sites.
source: Not all C. elegans TFs currently have well-defined binding sites and, as such, our analysis likely underestimates the number of regulators of neuronal identity.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study.

claim: The analysis likely underestimates the number of regulators of neuronal identity.
source: Not all C. elegans TFs currently have well-defined binding sites and, as such, our analysis likely underestimates the number of regulators of neuronal identity.
evidence: This is a stated limitation based on incomplete motif data.

claim: 94 DNA binding motifs (41% of 215 available motifs) were excluded because they were highly similar to other C. elegans TFs.
source: Moreover, we excluded 94 DNA binding motifs (41% of 215 available motifs) that were highly similar to other C. elegans TFs to avoid ambiguous motif signatures where one or more TFs may use the same binding site.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice to avoid ambiguity.

claim: In vitro derived DNA binding sites may not take into account the possibility that binding sites may differ in vivo.
source: Also, our (partial) reliance on in vitro derived DNA binding sites does not take into account the possibility that binding sites may differ in vivo.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of using in vitro binding data.

claim: The analysis provides strong support for the terminal selector model of neuron type specification.
source: In spite of these limitations, our analysis provides strong support for the terminal selector model of neuron type specification and it provides a rich resource for future experimentation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: The analysis provides a rich resource for future experimentation.
source: In spite of these limitations, our analysis provides strong support for the terminal selector model of neuron type specification and it provides a rich resource for future experimentation.
evidence: This is a stated outcome of the study.

claim: Many vertebrate TFs are utilized at multiple distinct steps during development, including early progenitor specification.
source: One general problem in revealing functions of TFs during terminal differentiation in more complex organisms is that many TFs are often utilized at multiple distinct steps during development, including early progenitor specification.
evidence: This is a general statement about vertebrate development.

claim: Simple, non-temporally controlled mutant analysis will obscure later functions of TFs in vertebrates.
source: Hence, simple, non-temporally controlled mutant analysis will obscure later functions.
evidence: This is a logical inference about experimental limitations.

claim: Vertebrate HOX cluster genes have functions in early patterning of the spinal cord.
source: For example, vertebrate HOX cluster genes have functions in early patterning of the spinal cord, but their function and expression during later stages of terminal differentiation have, surprisingly, remained unstudied.
evidence: This is a statement about known HOX gene functions.

claim: The function and expression of vertebrate HOX cluster genes during later stages of terminal differentiation have remained unstudied.
source: For example, vertebrate HOX cluster genes have functions in early patterning of the spinal cord, but their function and expression during later stages of terminal differentiation have, surprisingly, remained unstudied.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in knowledge.

claim: TargetOrtho2 employs the BEDOPS software for assignment of motif match coordinates to adjacent annotated coding genes.
source: We implement the BEDOPS software (Neph et al., 2012) for assignment of motif match coordinates to adjacent annotated coding genes.
evidence: This describes a component of the TargetOrtho2 methodology.

claim: BEDOPS allows a search of full intergenic and intronic regions when assigning a motif match to adjacent gene loci.
source: BEDOPS allows a search of full intergenic and intronic regions when assigning a motif match to adjacent gene loci.
evidence: This describes a capability of the BEDOPS software.

claim: Binding sites in downstream and exonic regions are annotated and output with TargetOrtho2 results but these values are not used for ranking of candidate TF target genes.
source: Binding sites in downstream and exonic regions are also annotated and output with TargetOrtho2 results but these values are not used for ranking of candidate TF target genes.
evidence: This describes what data is included but not used in the analysis.

claim: The GPC classifier has median recall of 0.8 and median rank sums test Z score of 6.06 (p<1e-9).
source: We found that a GPC modeled on the combined motif data from all three terminal selectors is the most accurate for the classification problem at hand (median recall = 0.8, median rank sums test Z score = 6.06, p<1e-9) with the most informative features being upstream and intronic motif match frequency, max log-odds motif score in upstream and intronic regions, plus upstream and intron motif match conservation among the eight nematode genomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative performance metric from the cross-validation analysis.

claim: The most informative features for the GPC classifier are upstream and intronic motif match frequency, max log-odds motif score in upstream and intronic regions, plus upstream and intron motif match conservation among the eight nematode genomes.
source: We found that a GPC modeled on the combined motif data from all three terminal selectors is the most accurate for the classification problem at hand (median recall = 0.8, median rank sums test Z score = 6.06, p<1e-9) with the most informative features being upstream and intronic motif match frequency, max log-odds motif score in upstream and intronic regions, plus upstream and intron motif match conservation among the eight nematode genomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the feature selection results.

claim: With increasing number of TF-dependent markers identified, the probability of identifying motif enrichment and significant ranking of neuron class-specific genes increases.
source: Examination of putative terminal selectors with available genetic loss-of-function data (Supplementary file 2A: genetic markers) shows that with increasing number of TF-dependent markers identified (and hence increasing confidence that the TF is a terminal selector), the probability of identifying motif enrichment and significant ranking of neuron class-specific genes from Wormbase also increases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) suggesting that the GPC classifier is appropriately identifying target genes from novel TF motifs.
evidence: This is an analysis validating the classifier performance.

claim: The GPC classifier is appropriately identifying target genes from novel TF motifs.
source: Examination of putative terminal selectors with available genetic loss-of-function data (Supplementary file 2A: genetic markers) shows that with increasing number of TF-dependent markers identified (and hence increasing confidence that the TF is a terminal selector), the probability of identifying motif enrichment and significant ranking of neuron class-specific genes from Wormbase also increases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) suggesting that the GPC classifier is appropriately identifying target genes from novel TF motifs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the validation analysis.

claim: HLH-4 regulates ADL identity.
source: Examination of another well-characterized terminal selector, HLH-4 that regulates ADL identity (Masoudi et al., 2018), shows significant enrichment and ranking of previously characterized hlh-4 target genes in ADL (Figure 4) further supporting the use of the GPC trained on three terminal selector's motif feature data.
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: HLH-4 target genes in ADL show significant enrichment and ranking by TargetOrtho2.
source: Examination of another well-characterized terminal selector, HLH-4 that regulates ADL identity (Masoudi et al., 2018), shows significant enrichment and ranking of previously characterized hlh-4 target genes in ADL (Figure 4) further supporting the use of the GPC trained on three terminal selector's motif feature data.
evidence: This is a validation result supporting the classifier.

claim: The Brain Atlas contains data for all 118 neuron classes.
source: This data is based on published reporter gene expression profiles and is a representative readout of the regulatory state of each neuron type. Since then, additional expression patterns have become available and we updated Brain Atlas. Our latest version contains data for all 118 neuron classes, with each neuron class expressing on average 50 reporter genes (range 14 to 233).
evidence: This describes the content of the Brain Atlas dataset.

claim: Taylor et al., 2019 identified 118 neuron class clusters from scRNA of FACS sorted neurons from L4 animals.
source: Aided by the molecular markers of neuronal identity from Brain Atlas, Taylor et al., 2019 identified 118 neuron class clusters from scRNA of FACS sorted neurons from L4 animals.
evidence: This describes the source of the single cell RNA-seq data.

claim: The VD and DD neuron classes did not separate into distinct clusters in the scRNA analysis.
source: The VD and DD neuron classes did not separate into distinct clusters. These are analyzed together as one VD_DD cluster in the analysis.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the clustering analysis.

claim: 136 neuronally expressed TFs with sufficiently unique DNA binding motifs were investigated.
source: Here, we further investigate 136 neuronally expressed TFs with sufficiently unique DNA binding motifs (see motif curation procedure below) as assessed by similarity regression (SR) scores comparing C. elegans TF DNA binding domains (Lambert et al., 2019) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the scope of TFs analyzed.

claim: Four motifs analyzed were defined and validated through a combination of in vitro and in vivo studies (UNC-3, CEH-10/TTX-3, CHE-1, HLH-4 DNA binding motifs).
source: Four other motifs analyzed here were defined and validated through a combination of in vitro and in vivo studies (UNC-3, CEH-10/TTX-3, CHE-1, HLH-4 DNA binding motifs) (Etchberger et al., 2007; Kratsios et al., 2011; Masoudi et al., 2018; Wenick and Hobert, 2004; Figure 2D, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This describes the source of four specific motifs.

claim: 389 neuronal TFs were identified from the set of differentially expressed TFs from single cell profiling and Wormbase reporters expressed in the nervous system.
source: Starting from the set of differentially expressed TFs from single cell profiling and Wormbase reporters expressed in the nervous system (Brain Atlas, Supplementary file 1C), we identified 389 neuronal TFs.
evidence: This describes the initial set of TFs considered.

claim: 214 neuronal TFs have available DNA binding motifs from the CISBP database version 2.00.
source: Using the CISBP database version 2.00 (Weirauch et al., 2014) to identify the best available motif from direct experimental evidence (or from the best inferred motif if no direct experimental motif exists), 214 neuronal TFs have available DNA binding motifs.
evidence: This describes the number of TFs with available motifs.

claim: An SR score cutoff of 0.807 was used to exclude motifs from TFs with highly similar DNA binding domains.
source: We used an SR score cutoff of 0.807, the lowest score that allowed us to include unc-42, a homeodomain TF in our analysis which has a DNA binding domain most similar to ceh-17 (SR score = 0.807).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice for motif selection.

claim: UMI count data from Taylor et al., 2021 for neuron type clusters were normalized using the SCTransform function in the Seurat 3.0 package.
source: UMI count data provided by Taylor et al., 2021 for neuron type clusters were normalized using the SCTransform function in the Seurat 3.0 package (Butler et al., 2018; Stuart et al., 2019) followed by differential expression analysis using the findMarkers function with the Wilcoxon test (log-fold change threshold = 0, adjusted p-value threshold < 0.05).
evidence: This describes the data processing methodology.

claim: Differential expression analysis was performed using the findMarkers function with the Wilcoxon test (log-fold change threshold = 0, adjusted p-value threshold < 0.05).
source: UMI count data provided by Taylor et al., 2021 for neuron type clusters were normalized using the SCTransform function in the Seurat 3.0 package (Butler et al., 2018; Stuart et al., 2019) followed by differential expression analysis using the findMarkers function with the Wilcoxon test (log-fold change threshold = 0, adjusted p-value threshold < 0.05).
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis methodology.

claim: Neuron subclass clusters were combined prior to differential expression analysis.
source: Neuron subclass clusters were combined prior to the differential expression analysis (ASEL and ASER combined into ASE, IL2_DV and IL2_LR combined into IL2, etc.) then each neuron class was tested against all other neuron classes (see Figure 2 for a full list of neuron classes analyzed).
evidence: This describes a data processing step.

claim: Motif analysis was performed for each TF with an unambiguous motif in each neuron class gene battery where the TF is expressed.
source: Motif analysis was performed for each TF with an unambiguous motif (Supplementary file 1A, exclusion_rule = None) in each neuron class gene battery where the TF is expressed.
evidence: This describes the scope of the motif analysis.

claim: Two tests were performed for each motif in each expressing neuron class gene battery: hypergeometric test for motif enrichment and Wilcoxon rank sums test.
source: Two tests were performed for each motif in each expressing neuron class gene battery: (a) hypergeometric test for motif enrichment and (b) Wilcoxon rank sums test.
evidence: This describes the statistical tests used.

claim: p-Values were corrected for multiple testing using the Benjamini/Hochberg method with alpha = 0.05.
source: p-Values were corrected for multiple testing using the Python statsmodels library multipletests function (method Benjamini/Hochberg, alpha = 0.05).
evidence: This describes the multiple testing correction methodology.

claim: Cofactor motif analysis was performed pairwise on all TFs expressed in each neuron class.
source: Cofactor motif analysis was performed pairwise on all TF expressed in each neuron class.
evidence: This describes the scope of the cofactor analysis.

claim: The marker population overlap per neuron class between single cell and Brain Atlas datasets varies from 0% to 11%, average 4.5%.
source: A comparison between single cell and Brain Atlas datasets shows that the proportion of genes with motifs per neuron class is highly correlated (Spearman correlation = 0.80, p=0) (Figure 8A) despite the independent nature of each dataset (marker population overlap per neuron class varies from 0% to 11%, average 4.5%).
evidence: This quantifies the overlap between the two datasets.

claim: ztf-11 is a TF implicated in neuronal transdifferentiation.
source: When panneuronally expressed regulators are included in this comparison, we find 92% agreement; this increase appears to be driven by ztf-11, a TF implicated neuronal transdifferentiation (Lee et al., 2019), predicted to have a coordinated regulatory role in 73 neuron classes.
evidence: This is cited from a published study.

claim: ztf-11 is predicted to have a coordinated regulatory role in 73 neuron classes.
source: When panneuronally expressed regulators are included in this comparison, we find 92% agreement; this increase appears to be driven by ztf-11, a TF implicated neuronal transdifferentiation (Lee et al., 2019), predicted to have a coordinated regulatory role in 73 neuron classes.
evidence: This is a result from the motif analysis.

claim: The processing time for analyzing 100 plus neuronal TF motifs was reduced from 91 to 1.8 days with TargetOrtho2.
source: This improvement in job processing time made this study possible with a reduction in processing time for the 100 plus neuronal TF motifs examined from 91 to 1.8 days.
evidence: This quantifies the computational improvement.

claim: Increased processing time was achieved by switching from Python's sqlite3-based database programming to Pandas library.
source: Increased processing time was achieved by switching from Python's sqlite3-based database programming to Pandas library.
evidence: This describes the technical change that improved performance.

claim: TargetOrtho2 runs on OS X or Linux operating systems.
source: The updated TargetOrtho2 software runs on OS X or Linux operating systems (Figure 3C).
evidence: This describes the software compatibility.

claim: Coordinated control of terminal gene batteries by terminal selector TFs is the major mode by which neuronal identity specification is achieved in C. elegans.
source: Hence, a coordinated regulatory control mechanism appears to be the major mode by which neuronal identity specification is achieved in C. elegans.
evidence: This is a major conclusion from the comprehensive analysis.

claim: Not every gene battery member contains high-scoring, well-conserved binding sites for terminal selectors.
source: Even though there is a significant enrichment of binding sites for terminal selectors in neuron type-specific gene batteries, not every gene battery member contains high-scoring, well-conserved binding sites.
evidence: This is an observation from the motif analysis.

claim: Some gene battery members may be regulated by non-conventional binding or indirect regulation via intermediary factors.
source: This could indicate either non-conventional binding or indirect regulation via intermediary factors.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for genes without high-scoring binding sites.

claim: The enrichment of binding sites and extensive past genetic loss-of-function analysis underscore the predominant role of terminal selectors in neuronal identity control.
source: The enrichment of bindings sites – as well as extensive past genetic loss-of-function analysis – clearly underscores the predominant role of terminal selectors in neuronal identity control.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating computational and genetic evidence.

claim: Co-expressed terminal selectors with coordinated regulatory motif signatures mainly target common effector genes.
source: For 16 out of these 17 cases, we observed significant co-enrichment and ranking of TargetOrtho2-predicted target genes, suggesting that co-expressed terminal selectors with coordinated regulatory motif signatures mainly target common effector genes (Figure 7B Supplementary file 2D).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the cofactor analysis.

claim: Combinatorial activity of TFs is the predominant mode of effector gene regulation.
source: Of these candidate terminal selector pairs (where motif 1 and motif 2 have a coordinated regulatory motif signature), we find that 98% show common target genes suggesting that a combinatorial activity of TFs is the predominant mode of effector gene regulation (Figure 7C, D, E, Figure 7—source data 1, Supplementary file 2G).
evidence: This is a major conclusion from the cofactor analysis.

claim: The cooperative function of unc-42 and unc-3 in specifying command interneuron identity is validated in an accompanying manuscript.
source: In an accompanying manuscript, we validate such cooperative function of unc-42 and unc-3 in specifying command interneuron identity (Berghoff et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from an accompanying manuscript.

claim: The analysis provides a blueprint for how individual components of an entire nervous system are genetically specified.
source: Our analysis provides a blueprint for how individual components of an entire nervous system are genetically specified.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a major outcome of the study.

claim: The likelihood of a TF binding site bearing relevance for the activation of a nearby gene is much increased if a site is phylogenetically conserved in the cross-species orthologs of that gene.
source: We reasoned that the likelihood of a TF binding site bearing relevance for the activation of a nearby gene is much increased if a site is phylogenetically conserved in the cross-species orthologs of that gene.
evidence: This is the rationale for the phylogenetic footprinting approach.

claim: Orthologous genes in C. elegans and C. briggsae that contain conserved copies of the AIY motif were confirmed to be expressed in AIY.
source: Orthologous genes in C. elegans and C. briggsae that contain conserved copies of the AIY motif were indeed confirmed to be expressed in AIY (Bigelow et al., 2004; Wenick and Hobert, 2004).
evidence: This is cited validation of the phylogenetic footprinting approach.

claim: In vitro derived DNA binding motifs used in this study predict biologically relevant TF binding sites.
source: The requirement of these binding sites for expression of this cholinergic neuronal identity gene supports our predicted terminal selector role for unc-86, lim-4, and unc-42 in URX, SMB, and SMD neuron classes, respectively, and also demonstrates that in vitro derived DNA binding motifs used in this study predict biologically relevant TF binding sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the binding site mutation experiments.
